title: Architecture Governance: Advice, Guardrails and Mandates

know: The author's three instruments from Grounded Architecture: nudges, taxes and mandates, with advice as the default.
The advice process and architecture decision records.
How the right instrument changes with scale and with the cost of divergence.
believe: A mandate is the most expensive instrument and should be the rarest.
An architect's job is to connect levels and inform decisions, more than to make them.
can_do: Choose an instrument for a given technical decision and justify it by the cost of divergence.
Write a decision record others can find and overturn.
Recognize governance that has become a review bottleneck.

audience.who: Executives (CTO, VP Engineering, Director) who must decide how technical direction is governed, and engineers and architects who want to follow the reasoning.
already_knows: How software teams work: services, deployment, code review, on-call
From the Part IV introduction and chapter 13: an engineering strategy is a diagnosis and a small set of policies that settle recurring decisions
The book's failure-pattern names and its three scarce capacities (attention, judgment, verification)

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given four technical decisions, the reader assigns each an instrument and gives the reason.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Assign advice, nudge, tax or mandate to each and say why: (1) which test framework a team uses; (2) whether services may store customer data outside the approved regions; (3) adopting a second programming language; (4) using the shared logging format.
acceptance_criteria.expected: (1) advice or none: local, cheap to diverge; (2) mandate: legal exposure; (3) tax or advice process with a decision record: the team bears the operating cost; (4) nudge via a paved path, mandate only if incidents show the cost.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter says how governance relies on the staff-plus roles defined in chapter 21 and links to it.
Concepts taken from a named source name the book and the concept; rules of thumb are presented as that author's rule of thumb; anything applied beyond the source is marked as the author's extension.
Each pattern in the chapter names its user and an outcome measure by which a reader could tell that it worked.

thesis.question: Who decides technical direction, and with how much force?
thesis.claim: Technical direction should be decided as close to the work as the cost of divergence allows: by default the team decides after seeking advice and records the decision; where consistency pays, the organization nudges with a paved path or taxes the divergent choice with the cost it imposes on others; and it mandates only where divergence creates risk the team cannot carry, such as legal exposure or security.
thesis.disputed_by: The architecture-board model, in which a central group approves designs before work starts because consistency and risk control require it.
thesis.so_what: A leader replaces most approvals with advice and records, keeps a short written list of mandates with reasons, and measures governance by how long a decision waits.
thesis.how_why: A central approver is a queue at the point where verification is scarcest, and it sees each decision with less information than the team. Instruments that change the cost of a choice leave the decision with the team and still move the landscape, and they scale with the number of teams where a board does not.

supporting_claims.claim: A central board that approves designs is the wrong default: it is a queue at the point where verification is scarcest, and it decides with less information than the team.
The default is advice and a record: the team decides after seeking advice from the people affected and the people with expertise, and writes a decision record that others can find and overturn.

Where a team's choice puts cost on others, the organization changes the cost of the choice with a nudge or a tax and leaves the decision with the team; it mandates only where divergence creates risk the team cannot carry, and a mandate is the most expensive of the instruments.
The instrument is chosen by the cost of divergence, is raised only on evidence, and the mix of instruments changes as the organization grows.
Governance of this kind is carried by senior technical leaders who connect levels and inform decisions more than they make them, and it is judged by how long a decision waits.

role.contribution: Says how the strategy's policies are enforced without creating a review bottleneck.

additional_patterns.applies_to: advice-and-record, three-instruments: the instruments are introduced from the least force to the most
three-instruments, choosing-the-instrument, who-carries-governance: the instruments are defined before the procedure that chooses among them, and the procedure before the roles that run it

flow.rationale: The reader first meets a board that is slow and still fails to produce consistency, then the reason a board behaves so, then the default that replaces it, then the stronger instruments for the cases the default does not cover, then how to choose among them, then who carries the work. Failures come after the model because two of the three are failures of the replacement. The worked example comes after everything it uses and returns to the opening case. Choosing before defining would be choosing by name; the roles before the instruments would be a job description with no work in it. The reason a board fails comes before the default because the default is derived from the two faults; put after it, advice would read as a preference. The failures come after the roles because the veto without a record and the growing rulebook are failures of the people who carry governance.

hook.content: In the first half of 2026 Corvane's architecture forum approved 33 of the 36 designs put to it, after a median wait of 23 days, and the company still ran four ways of deploying, three message brokers and two identity libraries.

bridge.from_reader_world: Most readers have waited for an architecture review, or sat on one, and have seen a landscape that the reviews did not keep consistent.
bridge.to_topic: Both the wait and the divergence come from asking one group to approve; the question is who should decide technical direction, and with how much force.

thesis_statement.text: Technical direction should be decided as close to the work as the cost of divergence allows: by default the team decides after seeking advice and records the decision; where consistency pays the organization nudges or taxes; it mandates only where divergence creates risk the team cannot carry.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

roadmap.placement: IN THIS CHAPTER callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

promises.promise: See Corvane's forum and the broker request it could not decide well.
Understand why a central approving board is the wrong default.
Learn the default: the advice process and the decision record.
Learn the three stronger instruments, nudge, tax and mandate, and how to choose among them by the cost of divergence.
Follow the broker decision at Corvane.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Corvane's architecture forum approved nearly every design after weeks of waiting and the landscape diverged anyway, and now three teams want a new message broker.

evidence.what: Corvane, 2026, about 500 people, about thirty teams: 33 of 36 designs approved, median wait 23 days; four ways of deploying, three message brokers, two identity libraries; three teams ask for a new broker.
evidence.shows: A board can be both slow and ineffective, which is the puzzle the chapter resolves.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Technical direction should be decided as close to the work as the cost of divergence allows, through advice and a record by default, a nudge or a tax where consistency pays, and a mandate only for risk a team cannot carry; the chapter takes these in order.

transition_in.carries_over: A forum that is slow and a landscape that still diverged; from the previous chapter, policies that settle recurring decisions and the open question of how they are applied across many teams.
transition_in.introduces: The instruments of governance, from advice to mandate, the record that holds each decision, and the route through the chapter.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene: A Forum That Approves and a Landscape Nobody Chose
sections.controlling_idea: At Corvane in 2026 an architecture forum approved nearly every design, late, while the landscape diverged anyway, and a request for a new message broker showed that the forum had neither the speed nor the information to decide it.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the case the chapter's opposing view produces: a board that is a queue and still does not produce consistency.

flow.rationale: The forum's rule comes first, then what a year of it produced, then the request that arrives into it; the request only reads as a problem once the queue is known.

transition_in.carries_over: The lead's short account of the forum and the broker.
transition_in.introduces: The situation in full: the rule, its results and the request.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Corvane's architecture forum, set up in 2025, was a meeting of senior engineers that had to approve any design that added a technology or changed an interface between teams before work started.

evidence.what: Corvane, 2025–2026, about 500 people, about thirty teams. Dario Vance, VP Engineering, sets up the forum in 2025; a meeting of senior engineers (ledger, chapter 13) chaired by Samir Haddad, attended by whoever else could come; meets every second week and hears three designs a meeting.
evidence.shows: Sets the rule whose effects the next paragraph counts.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In the first half of 2026 the forum approved 33 of 36 designs, 27 of them unchanged, after a median wait of 23 days, and the landscape still held four ways of deploying, three message brokers and two identity libraries.

evidence.what: Illustrative figures: 36 designs submitted in the first half of 2026, 33 approved, 27 unchanged, median wait 23 days from submission to hearing. Ledger (chapter 13): eleven requests in 2025–2026 for a new way of deploying, messaging or checking identity, most granted. Ledger: four ways of deploying, three message brokers, two identity libraries in 2026.
evidence.shows: An approving board can be slow and still not produce consistency, because each design is judged alone.

transition_in.introduces: What a year of the rule produced.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three teams asked for a new message broker while two others still used the oldest one, and the forum discussed the request in three sessions over six weeks without deciding, with less knowledge of the need than the teams asking.

evidence.what: Ledger: three teams want a new message broker that can replay messages; two others use the oldest one; the forum discussed it in three sessions over six weeks with different attendees and did not decide (chapter 13). New: the three are Dispatch, Notifications and Technician App; the two are Billing Integrations and Stock Integrations, which receive schedule-change events.
evidence.shows: Poses the chapter's question on one concrete decision: who decides, and with how much force.

transition_in.carries_over: A queue that approves nearly everything.
transition_in.introduces: The request that the rest of the chapter follows.

sections.heading: Why a Central Board Is the Wrong Default
sections.controlling_idea: A central approving board answers a real need for consistency and risk control with the wrong mechanism: it queues decisions where verification is scarcest and makes them with less information than the team has.

advances_thesis.how: Argues the first supporting claim against the view the thesis disputes, after stating that view's case.

flow.rationale: The board's case is stated first so that the two objections answer it; the principle that replaces it comes last because it is derived from the two objections.

transition_in.introduces: Why a board produces those results wherever it is set up.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The board model exists for a good reason: some technical choices should be made once for the whole company, and Enterprise Architecture as Strategy describes the classical mechanisms that enforce such choices, a compliance process, an exception process and a central standards team.

evidence.what: Ross, Weill and Robertson, Enterprise Architecture as Strategy: standardization brings efficiency and predictability and limits local innovation; the IT engagement model as 'the system of governance mechanisms' linking company-wide and project decisions; an architecture compliance process, an architecture exception process, a centralized standards team.
evidence.shows: The opposing view at its strongest, from the author's own notes on its best-known source.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A board that must approve is a queue at the point where verification is scarcest, because the designs to check grow with every team and the board does not; the book names this failure the Review Bottleneck, defined here as an interface built as an approval queue.

evidence.what: The book's failure pattern The Review Bottleneck (an interface designed as an approval queue); verification as one of the book's three scarce capacities; Corvane's 23 days and five people for thirty teams.
evidence.shows: Explains the wait as a property of the mechanism and not of the people on the board.

transition_in.introduces: What the board costs: a wait that grows with the number of teams.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The board also decides with less information than the team, so the chapter's principle is to decide as close to the work as the cost of divergence allows, where the cost of divergence is what one team's different choice costs other teams and the company.

evidence.what: Hohpe, The Software Architect Elevator: 'The worst-case scenario materializes when people holding relevant information or expertise aren't empowered to make decisions, whereas the decision makers lack relevant information.'
evidence.shows: Names the second fault of the board and motivates moving the decision to where the information is.

transition_in.introduces: The second fault, information, and the principle that follows from both.

sections.heading: Pattern: The Advice Process and the Decision Record
sections.controlling_idea: By default the team decides after seeking advice from the people affected and the people with expertise, and writes the decision in a record that anyone can find and a later decision can overturn.

advances_thesis.how: Supplies the default instrument and the record that holds every decision, whichever instrument is used.

flow.rationale: The advice process comes first because the record documents it; the record's parts come before the properties that make it findable and overturnable; the forum and the measure come last because they are how an organization runs the first three. The measure is its own unit because the worked example and the conclusion rely on it.

transition_in.carries_over: A decision that should sit near the work.
transition_in.introduces: The practice that leaves it there and still brings wider knowledge to it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In the advice process anyone may make an architectural decision provided they first seek advice from everyone meaningfully affected and from people with expertise; they must listen and record the advice, and they need not follow it.

evidence.what: Andrew Harmel-Law, 'Scaling the Practice of Architecture, Conversationally' (martinfowler.com, 15 December 2021), fetched and read: 'The Rule: anyone can make an architectural decision.'; the qualifier names two groups to consult; decision-takers are not obliged to agree; 'We are not looking for consensus here'.
evidence.shows: Defines the default instrument from a verified source.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A decision record is a page or two with a fixed set of parts, five from Michael Nygard's format plus the advice received and a condition for revisiting.

evidence.what: Seven rows: title, status, context, decision, consequences (Nygard, 'Documenting Architecture Decisions', 15 November 2011, fetched and read); advice received (Harmel-Law); revisit when (the author's addition). Columns: part, what it holds.
evidence.shows: Gives the reader the format they can write from.

transition_in.introduces: Where the advice and the decision are written down.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A record governs only if others can find it and overturn it: records sit in one searchable place with their status, and a decision is overturned by a new record that supersedes the old one, which is kept.

evidence.what: Nygard: records kept in the project repository; 'If a decision is reversed, we will keep the old one around, but mark it as superseded.' The author's records markdown-records and decisions-stay-with-teams.
evidence.shows: Shows what 'find and overturn' require in practice.

transition_in.introduces: The two properties that make a record an instrument of governance.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The pattern's users are the deciding team and the teams its decision affects, and a standing advisory forum, weekly and with no power to approve, gives them a place to ask.

evidence.what: Harmel-Law's Architecture Advisory Forum: weekly, decisions 'still owned and made by the originators'; the author's record architecture-advisory-forum.
evidence.shows: Names the pattern's users and the place where advice is sought.

transition_in.introduces: The forum that feeds it, who the pattern is for and how it is judged.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The pattern is judged by how long a decision waits, the days from a team's question to its recorded decision, kept honest by the share of records that list advice from outside the team.

evidence.what: The author's two measures: days from question to recorded decision; share of records listing outside advice. A short wait with no outside advice means teams have stopped asking.
evidence.shows: Gives the outcome measure the worked example and the conclusion use.

transition_in.carries_over: Who the pattern is for and where they ask.
transition_in.introduces: How one would know it worked.

sections.heading: Three Instruments Above Advice: Nudge, Tax and Mandate
sections.controlling_idea: When a team's choice puts cost on others, Grounded Architecture offers three stronger instruments, of which the nudge and the tax change the cost of a choice and leave it with the team, and the mandate removes the choice and costs the most.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the three instruments of the thesis and argues that the mandate should be the rarest.

flow.rationale: The instruments are defined from the least force to the most, because each is used only where the one before it does not suffice; the comparison table needs all four defined; the argument about the mandate's cost comes last because it compares the mandate with the other three.

transition_in.carries_over: Advice, which leaves a team free to choose.
transition_in.introduces: The cases where free choice puts cost on others, and three instruments for them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Advice does not stop a well-advised team from making a choice that is good for it and costly for others, and for that case Grounded Architecture describes governance as a portfolio of three influences: nudges, taxes and mandates.

evidence.what: Grounded Architecture, governance page: a hybrid governance model; nudges, taxes and mandates as 'a portfolio of influences rather than a single enforcement style'.
evidence.shows: Introduces the chapter's lead source and the three terms.
evidence.source: Željko Obrenović, Grounded Architecture, "Governance Principles: Nudges, Taxation, Mandates" (grounded-architecture.io/governance, read 2026-11-19)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A nudge makes the preferred choice the easy one without forbidding the others, and its main form in engineering is the paved path, a ready-made and supported way of doing a common task.

evidence.what: Thaler and Sunstein, Nudge: a nudge 'alters people's behavior in a predictable way without forbidding any options or significantly changing their economic incentives'; 'Default options thus act as powerful nudges.' Grounded Architecture applies it to golden paths, dashboards and principles.
evidence.shows: Defines the nudge from its source and names its engineering form.
evidence.source: Kindle notes, _input/bookshelf/docs/notes/nudge.pdf; Željko Obrenović, Grounded Architecture, "Governance Principles: Nudges, Taxation, Mandates" (grounded-architecture.io/governance, read 2026-11-19)

transition_in.introduces: The first and gentlest.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A tax leaves the choice with the team and makes the team pay the cost its choice puts on others; Grounded Architecture's example is charging cloud cost to the department that incurs it, and the author extends the idea to operating cost.

evidence.what: Grounded Architecture: taxation promotes accountability without prohibition; cross-charging public cloud costs. The author's extension: a team that diverges runs, upgrades and is on call for what it chose, and pays for the migration back.
evidence.shows: Defines the tax and marks what is extension.
evidence.source: Željko Obrenović, Grounded Architecture, "Governance Principles: Nudges, Taxation, Mandates" (grounded-architecture.io/governance, read 2026-11-19)

transition_in.carries_over: An instrument that changes how easy a choice is.
transition_in.introduces: One that changes what a choice costs the chooser.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A mandate states what teams must or must not do, and its best form is a guardrail, a limit checked automatically in the delivery path.

evidence.what: Grounded Architecture: mandates and bans are 'the most direct forms of governance', reserved for compliance, organizational priorities and strategic constraints. Guardrail as defined in the Part IV introduction; the author's record governance-as-code.
evidence.shows: Defines the third instrument and its automated form.
evidence.source: Željko Obrenović, Grounded Architecture, "Governance Principles: Nudges, Taxation, Mandates" (grounded-architecture.io/governance, read 2026-11-19); principles/governance-as-code

transition_in.carries_over: Two instruments that leave the choice with the team.
transition_in.introduces: The one that removes it, and all four compared.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Side by side, the four instruments differ in who decides, in how each acts and in what each costs the organization.

evidence.what: Four rows (advice, nudge, tax, mandate) by who decides, how it acts, an example and what it costs the organization.
evidence.shows: Puts the four instruments side by side before the argument about the mandate's cost.

transition_in.carries_over: Three instruments defined, and advice before them.
transition_in.introduces: All four compared.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A mandate is the most expensive instrument because it must be enforced and its exceptions handled, it overrides the team's information, and it hides whether the mandated thing is any good, so mandates belong on a short written list with reasons.

evidence.what: Grounded Architecture says mandates should be used sparingly and as a last resort; the three costs are the author's argument. The third is the reason chapter 15 gives for platforms earning adoption.
evidence.shows: Argues the belief 'a mandate is the most expensive instrument and should be the rarest'.
evidence.source: Željko Obrenović, Grounded Architecture, "Governance Principles: Nudges, Taxation, Mandates" (grounded-architecture.io/governance, read 2026-11-19)

transition_in.carries_over: The table's last row and last column.
transition_in.introduces: Why the mandate's cost is the highest, and what to do about it.

sections.heading: Choosing the Instrument by the Cost of Divergence
sections.controlling_idea: The instrument for a decision is chosen by asking who bears the cost if a team diverges, it is raised only when evidence shows the weaker one failed, and the mix changes as the organization grows.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the instruments into a procedure the reader can apply to any technical decision.

flow.rationale: The three questions come first, then four decisions sorted by them, then the rule for changing an instrument once chosen, then how the whole mix shifts with size, and last who the instruments serve and how they are judged, which closes the section; each step uses the one before.

transition_in.introduces: How to pick one for a given decision.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three questions in order choose the instrument: can the team carry the risk of diverging, does the cost of diverging fall on others, and can a paved path make the common choice the easy one.

evidence.what: Mermaid decision flow, Figure 1: risk the team cannot carry → mandate, as a guardrail where it can be checked; cost stays inside the team → the team decides, advice optional; cost falls on others → advice process and a record, plus a nudge where a paved path exists or is worth building, plus a tax on the divergent choice.
evidence.shows: Gives the reader the selection procedure in one picture.
evidence.source: the author's synthesis of Grounded Architecture's three instruments

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Four decisions sorted by the three questions show the range: a date library, personal data in logs, a new database engine and the standard deployment path.

evidence.what: Four rows by cost of divergence, instrument and reason: date-handling library (inside the team; team decides); personal data written to logs (legal exposure; mandate as a guardrail); a new database engine (falls on whoever operates and migrates it; advice process, record and tax); the standard deployment path (falls on every engineer who moves and every fix that must reach all paths; nudge by paved path, tax on leaving it).
evidence.shows: Demonstrates the procedure on cases the reader can compare with their own.

transition_in.introduces: Four decisions put through them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Start with the weakest instrument that could work and raise it only on evidence: when teams leave a paved path, the first question is what is wrong with the path, and a nudge becomes a mandate only when incidents or measured cost show that divergence is doing harm.

evidence.what: Thaler and Sunstein in the notes: 'If people know their preferences, and know that they dislike the outcome that is embedded in the default, they will probably change it.' The author's rule: low adoption is information about the path; incidents and measured cost are the evidence for a mandate; a mandate is reviewed and can be lowered.
evidence.shows: Gives the rule for moving between instruments, which the acceptance probe's fourth case needs.
evidence.source: Kindle notes, nudge.pdf; the author's recommendation

transition_in.introduces: When an instrument should be raised or lowered.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The mix of instruments changes with size, shown as what the author would expect at Corvane's five sizes: conversation at twelve people, advice and records at fifty, a paved path at 180, taxes, a mandate list with its first guardrails and an advisory forum at 500, and every checkable mandate as a guardrail at 1,100.

evidence.what: Five rows, one per Corvane stage (12, 50, 180, 500, 1,100 people): what changes and the instruments added. Stage sizes from the ledger; the mapping is the author's synthesis and an illustration.
evidence.shows: Shows that the right instrument depends on scale as well as on the decision.

transition_in.carries_over: When to raise or lower an instrument for one decision.
transition_in.introduces: The whole mix as an organization grows.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The users of the three instruments are the teams that choose and the teams that live with the result, and the instruments are working when most teams are on the paved paths by choice, the mandate list stays short and a decision does not wait.

evidence.what: The author's measures: share of teams on a paved path by choice; number of mandates on the list; decision wait.
evidence.shows: Names the user and the outcome measure for the nudge, tax and mandate, as the acceptance criteria ask.

transition_in.introduces: Whom the instruments serve at every size and how to tell they work.

sections.heading: Who Carries Governance: Architects as Connectors
sections.controlling_idea: Advice, paved paths and a mandate list are carried by senior technical leaders, whose job in governance is to connect levels and inform decisions more than to make them.

advances_thesis.how: Says who does the work the instruments need and links the technical leadership track of chapter 21.

flow.rationale: The dependence on the roles is stated first, then what the two sources say the role is, then the concrete jobs and how they are judged; the jobs are a list without the idea of the connector before them.

transition_in.carries_over: Instruments and a way to choose among them.
transition_in.introduces: The people without whom none of the instruments works.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: None of the instruments runs by itself: governance by advice relies on staff and principal engineers and architects, the staff-plus roles that chapter 21 defines.

evidence.what: Advice needs someone with cross-team knowledge to give it; a paved path needs someone to notice repeated advice; a mandate list needs an owner. Link to staff-plus-and-architects; the roles are not defined here.
evidence.shows: Meets the criterion that the chapter says how governance relies on the staff-plus roles and links chapter 21.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Hohpe and Grounded Architecture describe the architect as a connector: someone who moves between the level where strategy is set and the level where code is written, and holds architecture, technical detail, business needs and people together.

evidence.what: Hohpe, The Software Architect Elevator: 'instead of the superhero we need "super glue" architects'; the elevator between the penthouse and the engine room as Grounded Architecture's superglue page summarizes it; Grounded Architecture: 'Technical strength is necessary for architects, but it is rarely sufficient.'
evidence.shows: Supports the belief that the architect's job is to connect levels and inform decisions.

transition_in.introduces: What the two sources say the role is.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In governance these roles do four jobs, giving advice early, turning repeated advice into paved paths, keeping the mandate list short, and carrying what teams learn back to the strategy, and they are judged by the decisions they improved.

evidence.what: Grounded Architecture, general principles of the operating model: 'Architects should help teams make better decisions, not create approval queues.'; on mandates the architecture practice 'serves as a contributor—not the sole authority'. The four jobs and the measures are the author's summary.
evidence.shows: Names what the roles do, for whom, and how one would know it worked.

transition_in.introduces: The connector's four jobs in governance and their measure.

sections.heading: Anti-Patterns: The Gate, the Stall and the Growing Rulebook
sections.controlling_idea: Governance fails in three recognizable ways: approval returns under an advisory name, advice is mistaken for agreement, and the mandate list grows after every incident.

advances_thesis.how: Lets the reader recognize governance that has become a review bottleneck, and the two failures on the way from a board to advice.

flow.rationale: One paragraph per failure, ordered from the one the chapter opened with to the two that appear after a board has been replaced.

transition_in.introduces: Three ways it fails.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Review Bottleneck returns whenever teams wait for a forum before they act, whatever the forum is called, and three signs show it: finished designs are presented, nearly all are approved, and work waits for the hearing.

evidence.what: The failure pattern The Review Bottleneck; the author's record architecture-as-advice-and-guardrails lists the gate, the invisible veto and the record written afterwards.
evidence.shows: Gives the signs by which the reader recognizes the pattern.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Consensus Stall is the opposite error: the team treats advice as agreement to be reached and does not decide until every adviser concurs.

evidence.what: The failure pattern The Consensus Stall; Harmel-Law: 'We are not looking for consensus here, but we are looking for a broad range of inputs and voices.'
evidence.shows: Separates seeking advice from seeking consent.

transition_in.introduces: Waiting for everyone's agreement.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The growing rulebook is a mandate added after each incident and never removed, until teams cannot tell the three rules that protect the company from the thirty that record old preferences.

evidence.what: The author's observation, marked as such; the remedy is that every mandate names its reason and its owner and is reviewed on a rhythm.
evidence.shows: Shows how the most expensive instrument multiplies and how the list is kept short.

transition_in.introduces: A failure of mandates.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Corvane's New Broker
sections.controlling_idea: In 2026 Corvane's engineering strategy made the forum advisory and named shared areas, and the broker request was decided by the owner of the shared area through advice and a record, as a replacement with the migration of existing users planned before adoption.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the procedure to the case of the opening and gives the answer the Part IV criterion asks for.

flow.rationale: The change to the forum comes first because the broker decision runs through the new arrangement; then the advice, then what the record fixed, then the result.

transition_in.carries_over: The instruments, the procedure, the roles and the failures.
transition_in.introduces: All of them applied to the forum and the broker of the opening.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The engineering strategy Dario Vance wrote in 2026 changed the forum's rule from approval to advice and named three shared areas, and Corvane's decisions sorted by the cost of divergence give the mix the size table gave for 500 people.

evidence.what: Four rows (what stays inside a team's services; which way of deploying, broker or identity library a service uses; bringing a new technology into a shared area; where customer data is stored) by cost of divergence and instrument. Ledger (chapter 13): the 2026 strategy's rule of one standard per shared area with recorded, self-operated exceptions; a new technology enters a shared area only as a replacement; shared-area choices decided by the Director of Platform after written advice; the forum advises and does not vote. New: the reading of these as nudge, tax and mandate; customer data in approved regions as a mandate checked as a guardrail.
evidence.shows: Shows the procedure of the previous sections applied to a whole landscape before one decision is followed through it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because messaging is a shared area the decision sat with its owner, the Director of Platform, who decided by the advice process, and the advice changed the proposal from a fourth broker to a replacement.

sections.heading: What AI Changes Here
sections.controlling_idea: Coding agents make decision records and automated guardrails more useful and a human approval board less tenable, and the choice of AI tools is itself a governance decision sorted by the same three questions.

advances_thesis.how: Tests the chapter's argument against cheaper code production, with labeled claims.

flow.rationale: What is practised now comes before what may follow from it.

transition_in.carries_over: The governance model at human speed.
transition_in.introduces: The same model when agents write much of the code.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Emerging: teams that use coding agents give them decision records and paved-path templates as context, so a recorded decision reaches generated code that nobody told about it, and a rule that is an automated check applies to an agent's change as to a person's.

evidence.what: The author's observation as of November 2026, marked as such; no published measurement is cited, so no Proven claim is made.
evidence.shows: States what records and guardrails gain when agents write code.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Speculative: when agents multiply the number of changes, a board of people falls further behind and mandates that are not automated checks stop being enforced; Corvane's fourteen teams choosing their own agents in 2027–2028 show the three questions applied to AI tools.

evidence.what: Ledger: in 2027–2028 fourteen Corvane teams had each chosen their own coding agent, model provider and prompt conventions, and security could not say what data left the company. Reading: what data may leave the company is a mandate; which agent a team uses is a nudge by a supported default. Would be confirmed where review queues lengthen as change volume rises; chapter where-the-constraint-moves weighs the evidence.
evidence.shows: Applies the chapter's procedure to an AI decision and says what would confirm the claim.

transition_in.introduces: What is likely to follow, and one Corvane case.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The four instruments are one scale of force with one rule for reading it: the further the cost of a choice travels from the team that makes it, the more force the organization may use, and the record is what makes every point on the scale visible and reversible.
conclusion.so_what: A leader replaces most approvals with advice and records, keeps a short written list of mandates with reasons, and measures governance by how long a decision waits.

callback.to: Corvane's forum that approved 33 of 36 designs after 23 days, and the three teams' broker request.
callback.how: The reader can now say why the forum was slow and the landscape still diverged, and who should decide the broker with which instrument: the owner of the shared area, by advice and a record.

takeaway.content: List the approvals your teams wait for, sort each by the three questions, write the mandates that remain on one page with reasons and owners, and start measuring days from question to recorded decision.
